sentences.text: Panderichthys was a lobe-finned fish that lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 380 million years ago.
This animal measured between 1.5 and 2 meters in length and possessed a large, flattened, tetrapod-like head.
Its vertebral column was fully ossified with vertebrae comparable to those of early tetrapods, yet it retained an intracranial joint characteristic of fish.
The species shares ten specific anatomical features with tetrapods, including a flat skull roof, paired frontals, no external intracranial joint, and complex polyplocodont teeth.
Analysis of the humerus suggests that the evolutionary transition from fish-like limb structures to tetrapod limbs occurred more slowly than previously thought.
Researchers suggest Panderichthys may have used its pectoral fins to anchor itself while moving forward via side-to-side body undulation.
The small, finger-like bones in Panderichthys lack muscle development and joints, representing an intermediate form between fish fins and tetrapod limbs.
Panderichthys is considered at least a facultative air breather, representing an intermediate stage in the evolution of air breathing.
Due to its size and co-occurrence with bite-marked heterostracans, Panderichthys may have been a major predator of these armored jawless fish.
Fossils of Panderichthys were recovered from Frasnian deposits in Latvia.
The species Panderichthys rhombolepis was discovered by Gross in 1930, while Panderichthys stolbovi was discovered and illustrated by Emilia Vorobyeva in 1960.
The genus Panderichthys is named after the paleontologist Christian Heinrich Pander.
Panderichthys is hypothesized to have been adapted for moving in shallow, debris-filled waters in a marginal marine environment.
Researchers suggest Panderichthys may have used its pectoral fins to anchor itself while moving forward via side-to-side body undulation.
It is hypothesized that P. rhombolepis was a large predator feeding on dipterids, small and juvenile sarcopterygians, and Latvius.
Due to its size and co-occurrence with bite-marked heterostracans, Panderichthys may have been a major predator of these armored jawless fish.
The genus Panderichthys was described by Gross in 1941, and the type species is Panderichthys rhombolepis.
Recent studies redefine Elpistostegalia as a clade starting with Panderichthys and including all living tetrapods.
Its parent group is the family Panderichthyidae, and it is classified within the class Osteichthyes.
Panderichthys lived during the late Devonian (Frasnian) period in Lode, Latvia.
The genus lived from the Givetian to the Frasnian stages, between 387.95 and 372.15 million years ago.
The discovery of possible tetrapod tracks predating Panderichthys suggests that the genus was not a direct ancestor of tetrapods.
Panderichthys is considered the closest evolutionary relative to tetrapods that still possessed fins.
It was the ancestor of the first tetrapods, from which all other land vertebrates, including humans, descended.
